title: The Ben Franklin effect
hook: Want someone to like you more? Franklin's advice was to ask them for a favour.
peek: Benjamin Franklin wrote that he won over a political rival by asking to borrow a rare book from him. Psychologists later tested the idea: doing someone a kindness may make you like them more.
lede: In his autobiography, Benjamin Franklin describes a fellow member of the Pennsylvania legislature who opposed him. Rather than flatter the man, Franklin asked to borrow a rare book from his library. He returned it with a note of thanks, and the rival became friendly from then on. Franklin's lesson: someone who has done you a kindness is more likely to do you another.

bullets.text: Participants won money in a staged experiment, and some were then asked by the researcher to give it back as a personal favour. Those people later rated him more warmly. The study was small.
The usual explanation is that we dislike holding conflicting beliefs. If I helped you, I must like you, so my feelings shift to match my actions.
Later experiments have found similar effects, but they are not huge, and asking for too much can easily backfire. It is a nudge, not a guaranteed way to make friends.
